title: The Blaschka Object Network — Harvard Receiving Skill and Museum Practice Register
scope: Archival evidence for the receiving-side labour that converted transported Blaschka models into stable museum objects at Harvard: customs opening, unpacking, remounting, repair, labelling, display, photography and accumulated staff expertise. The register centres Louis Charles Bierweiler because both Blaschka correspondence and Harvard's finding aid identify him as a long-term museum technician/curator with direct workshop and object-handling experience.
methodological_guard: Biographical and museum-record files are not assumed to contain a report of every shipment. Direct handling claims come from dated Blaschka/Harvard correspondence; HOLLIS components are used to identify the archival universe for the actor and institutional practice. Later photographs and teaching-use records are evidence of continued custodial work, not proof of a specific 1930s repair unless the image/file says so.

actor.name: Louis Charles Bierweiler
roles: Harvard Botanical Museum curator / museum staff

direct_primary_evidence.evidence: Harvard correspondence sends Bierweiler to the Treasurer's Office to arrange prompt clearing of the incoming Blaschka shipment; after arrival he is associated with slight local repair.
Rudolf explicitly tells Bierweiler that some models in the recent shipment were complicated to unpack and compliments his skill and carefulness for the excellent result.

harvard_archive.collection: The Archives of Rudolf and Leopold Blaschka and the Ware Collection of Blaschka Glass Models of Plants
harvard_archive.collection_scope: Correspondence, manuscripts, curatorial files, artwork, photographs, publications, ephemera, artifacts, original boxes and mailing material documenting creation, growth and administration of the Glass Flowers.

related_institutional_archive.scope: Administrative, research, teaching and public-exhibition activities of the Museum.
related_institutional_archive.guard: The collection is broader than the Glass Flowers and has a late bulk date. It is indexed as a companion institutional archive for museum practice, not as a substitute for the Blaschka collection's direct shipment correspondence.

research_observation: The receiving institution acquired technique as well as objects. Bierweiler's 1931 visit to Hosterwitz collapses the apparent division between maker-side and museum-side knowledge: a Harvard curator entered the workshop, later coordinated clearance and repair, and was explicitly praised by Rudolf for skilled unpacking. The circulation system therefore transferred tacit handling knowledge through people, not only instructions attached to crates.
